# Autoencodix

AUTOENCODIX is a Python framework to train, evaluate, explain and share autoencoders for biological data and beyond (bulk and single-cell omics, images, any tabular data). All architectures share one pipeline API (preprocess, fit, predict, visualize, generate, evaluate, explain, save/load) and are configured with validated Pydantic configs; call `<Name>Config.print_schema()` to list all parameters. Pretrained models are on https://huggingface.co/autoencodix. Source: https://github.com/jan-forest/autoencodix_package


# Getting started

### One framework to train, evaluate, explain and share autoencoders for biological data and beyond

[Documentation](https://jan-forest.github.io/autoencodix_package/) · [Tutorials](#tutorials) · [Pretrained models](https://huggingface.co/collections/autoencodix/acx-pretrained-models) · [GitHub](https://github.com/jan-forest/autoencodix_package) · [Paper](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43588-025-00916-4)

______________________________________________________________________

**AUTOENCODIX** is a Python framework for representation learning with autoencoders. It was designed with biological data in mind but is general enough for any tabular, multi-modal or image data. A growing collection of architectures, from vanilla and variational autoencoders to ontology-constrained, disentangled, masked, multi-modal and imaging models, all share one pipeline API. Each pipeline covers the full workflow: preprocessing, training, tuning, embedding, generation, evaluation, visualization and explanation.

Autoencoders compress high-dimensional, non-linear and multi-modal measurements into a compact latent space. Examples include bulk and single-cell omics, medical and microscopy images, and other complex data. That latent space can be used for data integration, clustering, classification, imputation, cross-modal translation and synthetic data generation. Many autoencoder variants have been published, but each usually comes with its own code, data format and evaluation. AUTOENCODIX puts them in one place, so you can compare architectures fairly, reuse pretrained models and focus on your research question.

```
import autoencodix as acx

pipeline = acx.Varix(data=my_datapackage)   # pick any architecture
result = pipeline.run()                     # preprocess → fit → predict → visualize
```

## Highlights

- **Many architectures, one API.** Switching between architectures, for example from `Vanillix` to `Varix`, `Ontix` or `XModalix`, means changing a single class name. New architectures plug into the same pipeline.
- **Biology first, not biology only.** Native support for bulk and single-cell omics (`csv`, `parquet`, `h5ad`, `MuData`) and 2D/3D images (`tiff`, `jpg`, ...), in paired or unpaired multi-modal setups. Any other data that fits into a table or an image works the same way.
- **Pretrained models.** Ready-to-use single-cell encoders on the [Hugging Face Hub](https://huggingface.co/autoencodix) for embedding your own data without training.
- **Explainable by design.** Ontology-constrained latent spaces, feature-to-latent attributions with [Captum](https://captum.ai/), and LLM-assisted interpretation of latent dimensions.
- **Benchmark-informed defaults.** `propose_initial_config()` gives tuned starting configs derived from more than 100,000 benchmark training runs.
- **Reproducible.** Every setting lives in one validated (Pydantic) config. Runs can be fully seeded, and pipelines can be saved and reloaded.

## Core features

Every architecture is a **pipeline object** with the same set of steps. Call `.run()` to execute the standard sequence, or call the steps one by one for full control:

| Step                  | What it does                                                                       |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `.preprocess()`       | Reads, scales, filters and splits your data into train/valid/test                  |
| `.fit()`              | Trains the autoencoder and tracks losses per epoch and split                       |
| `.predict()`          | Encodes data into the latent space and reconstructs it                             |
| `.visualize()`        | Plots loss curves, latent embeddings and latent distributions                      |
| `.generate()`         | Samples new synthetic data from the latent space                                   |
| `.evaluate()`         | Benchmarks the embedding on downstream ML tasks                                    |
| `.explain()`          | Attributes latent dimensions to input features, optionally with LLM interpretation |
| `.save()` / `.load()` | Saves and restores the whole pipeline, including model, config and results         |

**Preprocessing.** Load tabular data (`csv`, `txt`, `parquet`), single-cell data (`h5ad`, `AnnData`/`MuData`) and images (`tiff`, `jpg`, `png`, 3D volumes) through one `DataPackage`. Built-in scaling, feature filtering (variance, correlation, NaN handling), single-cell filters and reproducible data splits work on any number of modalities.

**Training and tuning.** Training uses PyTorch and Lightning Fabric on CPU, GPU or multiple devices. You can set mixed precision, β-annealing schedules, and the layer and latent-space design. Hyperparameter optimization works with the built-in search or with [Optuna](https://optuna.org/), and `propose_initial_config()` gives you a strong starting point.

**Model hub: inference and generation.** Load pretrained models from the [Hugging Face Hub](https://huggingface.co/autoencodix), embed new samples with `.predict()`, classify or cluster them in the latent space, and create synthetic samples with `.generate()`.

**Evaluation and visualization.** Compare your latent space against PCA, UMAP, t-SNE or random features on downstream classification and regression tasks with any scikit-learn estimator (or TabPFN). Visualize embeddings, per-dimension latent distributions, and disentanglement metrics such as total correlation and coverage.

**Explainability.** Compute feature-to-latent attributions, such as gene-level importance, with DeepLIFT-SHAP or Integrated Gradients via [Captum](https://captum.ai/). The top features of each latent dimension can then be passed to an LLM (Mistral, Ollama, OpenRouter, ...) for a domain-level interpretation of the latent space.

## Architectures

| Pipeline                           | Type                     | Typical use case                         | Data                            | Key reference                                                                                                                                 |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [`Vanillix`](#vanillix)            | Autoencoder              | Non-linear dimension reduction, baseline | Tabular, multi-omics            | [Hinton & Salakhutdinov 2006](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1127647)                                                                        |
| [`Varix`](#varix)                  | Variational AE           | Smooth, generative latent space          | Tabular, single-cell            | [Kingma & Welling 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6114)                                                                                      |
| [`Ontix`](#ontix)                  | Ontology-constrained VAE | Interpretable latent dimensions          | Tabular, single-cell            | [Seninge et al. 2021](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-26017-0); [Doncevic & Herrmann 2023](https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btad387) |
| [`Disentanglix`](#disentanglix)    | Disentangled VAE         | Independent factors of variation         | Tabular, single-cell            | [Chen et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.04942)                                                                                          |
| [`Maskix`](#maskix)                | Masked AE                | Robust embeddings, imputation            | Tabular, single-cell            | [Fang et al. 2024](https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btae020)                                                                            |
| [`Supervisix`](#supervisix)        | Semi-supervised VAE      | Label-guided embeddings                  | Tabular, single-cell            | [Das et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.14865)                                                                                           |
| [`Stackix`](#stackix)              | Hierarchical VAE         | Multi-modal integration, unpaired data   | Multi-modal tabular             | [Simidjievski et al. 2019](https://doi.org/10.3389/fgene.2019.01205)                                                                          |
| [`XModalix`](#xmodalix)            | Cross-modal VAE          | Translation between modalities           | Tabular ↔ images                | [Yang & Uhler 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.03515)                                                                                         |
| [`Imagix`](#imagix-and-imagix3d)   | Convolutional VAE        | Image embeddings                         | 2D images                       | [Yang & Uhler 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.03515)                                                                                         |
| [`Imagix3D`](#imagix-and-imagix3d) | 3D convolutional VAE     | Volumetric embeddings                    | 3D images (CT, MRI, microscopy) | [Yang & Uhler 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.03515)                                                                                         |

### Vanillix

A classic fully connected autoencoder that compresses the input into a deterministic bottleneck and reconstructs it. **Use it** as a fast, robust baseline for non-linear dimension reduction and multi-modal integration, or when you just need a compact feature representation. **Strengths:** simple, few hyperparameters, quick to train. It is also the reference implementation of the shared pipeline, so start here.

**Based on:** Hinton & Salakhutdinov (2006). Reducing the dimensionality of data with neural networks. *Science* 313, 504–507. [doi:10.1126/science.1127647](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1127647)

### Varix

A variational autoencoder (VAE) that learns a probabilistic latent space (μ, σ) regularized toward a prior with a KL or MMD loss. **Use it** when you want a smooth, continuous latent space for clustering, trajectory analysis or generating synthetic samples. **Strengths:** a well-structured latent space, sampling-based generation, and β-annealing for a stable trade-off between reconstruction and regularization. Varix is the basis for most other architectures in the framework.

**Based on:** Kingma & Welling (2014). Auto-encoding variational Bayes. *ICLR*. [arXiv:1312.6114](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6114)

### Ontix

A VAE with a **sparse decoder whose connections follow an ontology or any other hierarchical feature grouping**. Examples are pathways → sub-pathways → genes, or chromosomes → cytobands → genes. Each latent dimension therefore corresponds to a named entity. **Use it** when interpretability matters, for example to read out pathway activity per sample or cell. **Strengths:** explainable by design, supports multi-level ontologies supplied as text files or Python dictionaries, and pairs naturally with `.explain()`.

**Based on:** Seninge et al. (2021). VEGA is an interpretable generative model for inferring biological network activity in single-cell transcriptomics. *Nat. Commun.* 12, 5684. [doi:10.1038/s41467-021-26017-0](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-26017-0) · Doncevic & Herrmann (2023). Biologically informed variational autoencoders allow predictive modeling of genetic and drug-induced perturbations. *Bioinformatics* 39(6), btad387. [doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/btad387](https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btad387) · Joas et al. (2025), see [Citation](#citation)

### Disentanglix

A disentangled VAE that splits the KL term into **mutual information, total correlation and dimension-wise KL**, each with its own weight (`beta_mi`, `beta_tc`, `beta_dimKL`). **Use it** when you want latent dimensions that capture independent factors of variation, for example separating cell type from disease state. **Strengths:** more independent and interpretable dimensions, fine-grained control over regularization, and built-in disentanglement metrics.

**Based on:** Chen et al. (2018). Isolating sources of disentanglement in variational autoencoders (β-TCVAE). *NeurIPS*. [arXiv:1802.04942](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.04942)

### Maskix

A masked autoencoder that randomly corrupts input entries and learns both to **reconstruct the original data and to predict which entries were masked**. **Use it** for sparse, noisy data such as single-cell transcriptomics, for robust embeddings, and for imputing missing values. **Strengths:** self-supervised denoising, good representations for clustering, and a built-in imputation method.

**Based on:** Fang et al. (2024). scMAE: a masked autoencoder for single-cell RNA-seq clustering. *Bioinformatics* 40(1), btae020. [doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/btae020](https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btae020)

### Supervisix

A semi-supervised VAE that adds **class-cohesion and class-separation losses** on top of the VAE objective, pulling samples toward their class center and pushing class centers apart. **Use it** when (partial) labels such as cell types, disease groups or any other class annotation are available and the latent space should reflect them. **Strengths:** label-aware embeddings that still model unlabeled samples, and better separation for downstream classification.

**Based on:** the cluster (center) loss of the semi-supervised VAE in Das, Lønfeldt, Pagsberg & Clemmensen (2022). Towards transferable speech emotion representation: on loss functions for cross-lingual latent representations. *ICASSP 2022*. [arXiv:2203.14865](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.14865)

### Stackix

A hierarchical (stacked) VAE: one **outer VAE per modality** learns a modality-specific latent space, and these latent spaces are concatenated and integrated by a **shared inner VAE**. **Use it** for integrating heterogeneous modalities such as multi-omics, especially when not every sample has every modality (`requires_paired=False`). **Strengths:** handles unpaired data, gives both per-modality and joint embeddings, and scales to many modalities.

**Based on:** Simidjievski et al. (2019). Variational autoencoders for cancer data integration: design principles and computational practice. *Front. Genet.* 10, 1205. [doi:10.3389/fgene.2019.01205](https://doi.org/10.3389/fgene.2019.01205) · Joas et al. (2025), see [Citation](#citation)

### XModalix

A cross-modal VAE that trains one encoder–decoder per modality and **aligns their latent spaces**, so that you can encode one modality and decode another. **Use it** to translate between data types, for example gene expression ↔ images, or to impute a missing modality. **Strengths:** works with paired and unpaired data, combines tabular and image modalities, and supports generation across modalities.

**Based on:** Yang & Uhler (2019). Multi-domain translation by learning uncoupled autoencoders. [arXiv:1902.03515](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.03515)

### Imagix and Imagix3D

Convolutional VAEs for **2D images** (`Imagix`) and **3D volumes** (`Imagix3D`, for example CT, MRI or volumetric microscopy). **Use them** to embed imaging data, compare image phenotypes with omics or other tabular profiles, or serve as the image branch of `XModalix`. **Strengths:** a standard and a fast architecture variant, flexible input sizes, and diagnostics for active latent dimensions.

**Based on:** Yang & Uhler (2019). Multi-domain translation by learning uncoupled autoencoders. [arXiv:1902.03515](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.03515). Imagix3D extends this design to 3D convolutions.

## Installation and quick start

### Installation

AUTOENCODIX requires Python ≥ 3.9 and < 3.13.

```
pip install autoencodix
```

To get the latest development version, use [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) (recommended):

```
git clone https://github.com/jan-forest/autoencodix_package.git
cd autoencodix_package
uv venv --python 3.10
source .venv/bin/activate
uv sync
```

### Train an autoencoder on your own data

```
import autoencodix as acx
from autoencodix.data.datapackage import DataPackage
from autoencodix.configs.vanillix_config import VanillixConfig
from autoencodix.configs.default_config import DataCase

# Tabular (non-single-cell) data goes into `multi_bulk`: one or more modalities as pandas DataFrames.
# With one annotation table per modality, use the same keys as in multi_bulk instead of "paired".
data = DataPackage(
    multi_bulk={"rna": raw_rna, "protein": raw_protein},
    annotation={"paired": annotation},
)

config = VanillixConfig(data_case=DataCase.MULTI_BULK, epochs=30, device="cpu")
pipeline = acx.Vanillix(data=data, config=config)
result = pipeline.run()

latent = result.get_latent_df(split="test", epoch=-1)   # sample × latent-dimension DataFrame
```

➡️ Full walkthrough: [Vanillix: Getting Started](https://jan-forest.github.io/autoencodix_package/tutorials/PipelineTutorials/Vanillix/index.md). Other data types (single-cell, images, unpaired data) are covered in [Input data](https://jan-forest.github.io/autoencodix_package/tutorials/DeepDives/InputDataTutorials/index.md), and all config options in [Configuration](https://jan-forest.github.io/autoencodix_package/tutorials/DeepDives/ConfigTutorial/index.md).

### Start from a benchmark-informed configuration

```
config = acx.propose_initial_config("varix")   # tuned hyperparameters instead of generic defaults
pipeline = acx.Varix(data=data, config=config)
```

➡️ Objectives, training budgets and overrides: [Propose initial config](https://jan-forest.github.io/autoencodix_package/tutorials/DeepDives/ProposeInitialConfigTutorial/index.md).

### Embed new data with a pretrained model

```
from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download
import autoencodix as acx

path = snapshot_download(repo_id="autoencodix/Varix-Dim32-Varix")
model = acx.Varix.load(file_path=f"{path}/large_varix_final_model_Dim32_Varix.pkl")
result = model.predict(data=my_dataset_container)
```

➡️ Data preparation, visualization and explanation: [Using Pretrained Models](https://jan-forest.github.io/autoencodix_package/tutorials/DeepDives/UsingPreTrainedModels/index.md). Available models are listed in [Pretrained models on Hugging Face](#pretrained-models-on-hugging-face).

### Go further

```
result = pipeline.evaluate(params=["CANCER_TYPE"], reference_methods=["PCA", "UMAP"])   # benchmark the embedding
attributions = pipeline.explain(method="IntegratedGradients")                            # feature-to-latent attributions
samples = pipeline.generate(n_samples=100)                                               # synthetic data
```

➡️ See the [Evaluate](https://jan-forest.github.io/autoencodix_package/tutorials/DeepDives/EvaluateTutorial/index.md) and [Explain](https://jan-forest.github.io/autoencodix_package/tutorials/DeepDives/ExplainStep/index.md) deep dives, and the [Tutorials](#tutorials) overview for all architectures.

## Pretrained models on Hugging Face

> **Skip training: use a pretrained single-cell encoder.** We publish ready-to-use AUTOENCODIX models in the [**acx-pretrained-models**](https://huggingface.co/collections/autoencodix/acx-pretrained-models) collection on the Hugging Face Hub. Download one with a single line and embed your own scRNA-seq data in minutes.

| Model family                       | Latent dims  | What you get                                    | Models                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------ | ----------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Varix**                          | 16 / 32 / 48 | General-purpose transcriptome embedding         | [Dim16](https://huggingface.co/autoencodix/Varix-Dim16-Varix) · [Dim32](https://huggingface.co/autoencodix/Varix-Dim32-Varix) · [Dim48](https://huggingface.co/autoencodix/Varix-Dim48-Varix)                                           |
| **Disentanglix**                   | 16 / 32 / 48 | Disentangled, independent latent factors        | [Dim16](https://huggingface.co/autoencodix/Disentanglix-Dim16-Disentanglix) · [Dim32](https://huggingface.co/autoencodix/Disentanglix-Dim32-Disentanglix) · [Dim48](https://huggingface.co/autoencodix/Disentanglix-Dim48-Disentanglix) |
| **Ontix** (GPT-5.6 ontology)       | 16 / 32 / 48 | Interpretable dimensions = biological processes | [Dim16](https://huggingface.co/autoencodix/Ontix-Dim16-GPT5-6) · [Dim32](https://huggingface.co/autoencodix/Ontix-Dim32-GPT5-6) · [Dim48](https://huggingface.co/autoencodix/Ontix-Dim48-GPT5-6)                                        |
| **Ontix** (Claude Opus 5 ontology) | 16 / 32 / 48 | Interpretable dimensions = biological processes | [Dim16](https://huggingface.co/autoencodix/Ontix-Dim16-ClaudeOpus5) · [Dim32](https://huggingface.co/autoencodix/Ontix-Dim32-ClaudeOpus5) · [Dim48](https://huggingface.co/autoencodix/Ontix-Dim48-ClaudeOpus5)                         |
| **Ontix** (Kimi K3 ontology)       | 16 / 32 / 48 | Interpretable dimensions = biological processes | [Dim16](https://huggingface.co/autoencodix/Ontix-Dim16-KimiK3) · [Dim32](https://huggingface.co/autoencodix/Ontix-Dim32-KimiK3) · [Dim48](https://huggingface.co/autoencodix/Ontix-Dim48-KimiK3)                                        |

All models are trained on a balanced collection of nearly **4 million cells** from the [CZ CELLxGENE](https://cellxgene.cziscience.com/) collection. A detailed description of the training data and models will follow in an upcoming preprint.

**What you can do with a pretrained model:**

- **Embed** your own cells (`AnnData`, Ensembl gene IDs, log1p-normalized counts). Missing genes are zero-padded automatically through a template.
- **Annotate and classify** cells in the latent space with any scikit-learn model.
- **Interpret** Ontix dimensions directly as biological processes, or run `.explain()` with LLM support.
- **Generate** synthetic cells with `.generate()`.
- **Fine-tune** a model on your own data *(planned, not yet natively supported)*.

Each model card has a copy-paste usage example. For a complete walkthrough, see the [Using Pretrained Models tutorial](https://jan-forest.github.io/autoencodix_package/tutorials/DeepDives/UsingPreTrainedModels/index.md).

The Hub also hosts the **tutorial datasets** ([TCGA](https://huggingface.co/datasets/autoencodix/tcga), [CELLxGENE lung](https://huggingface.co/datasets/autoencodix/census-lung), [pancreas](https://huggingface.co/datasets/autoencodix/pancreas-fang), [MNIST/MedMNIST](https://huggingface.co/datasets/autoencodix/mnist)) and the [benchmark-derived initial configs](https://huggingface.co/datasets/autoencodix/initial-configs). Tutorials download them automatically on first run.

## Tutorials

All tutorials are Jupyter notebooks that run on real data, which is downloaded automatically. They are also rendered in the [documentation](https://jan-forest.github.io/autoencodix_package/).

## Contributing: architectures and pretrained models

AUTOENCODIX is a community project. Its value grows with every architecture and every trained model that others can reuse. We particularly welcome:

**New architectures.** Have you published, or do you use, an autoencoder variant that is missing here? Every architecture builds on the same base classes (`BaseAutoencoder`, `BaseLoss`, `BaseTrainer`, `BasePipeline`). A new model only needs its architecture, loss and, if necessary, a custom trainer. Preprocessing, evaluation, visualization, explainability and saving come for free. The [Developer Guide](https://jan-forest.github.io/autoencodix_package/tutorials/DevGuide/index.md) explains how to add one.

**Pretrained models.** Have you trained an AUTOENCODIX model on an interesting atlas, tissue, organism, modality or a dataset outside biology? Share it with the community through the [autoencodix Hugging Face organization](https://huggingface.co/autoencodix). Open an issue and we will help you prepare a model card and add the model to the [pretrained collection](https://huggingface.co/collections/autoencodix/acx-pretrained-models).

**Everything else.** Bug reports, feature requests, tutorials, documentation fixes and benchmark datasets are all welcome.

How to get started:

1. Open an [issue](https://github.com/jan-forest/autoencodix_package/issues/new/choose) describing your idea, so that we can give early feedback.
1. Fork the repository, implement your change and add tests.
1. Open a [pull request](https://github.com/jan-forest/autoencodix_package/compare).

See [DEVELOPER.md](https://github.com/jan-forest/autoencodix_package/blob/main/DEVELOPER.md) for detailed guidelines, or reach us at [jan.ewald@uni-leipzig.de](mailto:jan.ewald@uni-leipzig.de).

## FAQ

**I get a `RuntimeError` about deterministic behavior and CuBLAS** When you request full reproducibility (`FIX_RANDOMNESS: "all"` / `reproducible=True`) on CUDA ≥ 10.2, PyTorch may raise:

```
RuntimeError: Deterministic behavior was enabled with either `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)` or `at::Context::setDeterministicAlgorithms(true)`, but this operation is not deterministic because it uses CuBLAS and you have CUDA >= 10.2.
```

Set this environment variable before running the pipeline (before `torch` is imported):

```
export CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG=:16:8
```

**Which architecture should I choose?** Start with `Vanillix` or `Varix` as a baseline, then pick a specialized architecture from the [Architectures](#architectures) table that matches your goal, such as interpretability, multi-modal integration, cross-modal translation or imputation. The `.evaluate()` step lets you compare them on your own data.

**Can I use AUTOENCODIX for non-biological data?** Yes. Anything you can load into a `pandas.DataFrame`, `AnnData` or `MuData`, or store as image files, can be passed via `DataPackage`. Biology-specific components such as ontologies or single-cell filters are optional. See the [Input data tutorial](tutorials/DeepDives/InputDataTutorials.ipynb).

# How to Train and Use Disentanglix: A Disentangled VAE[¶](#how-to-train-and-use-disentanglix-a-disentangled-vae)

`Disentanglix` is a variant of the `Varix` pipeline that implements a **disentangled variational autoencoder**.\
Its key difference lies in the loss function, which decomposes the standard VAE loss into subcomponents to encourage disentanglement in the latent space with independent latent dimensions.

**IMPORTANT**

> This tutorial only shows the specifics of the Disentanglix pipeline. If you're unfamiliar with general concepts,\
> we recommend following the `Getting Started - Vanillix` tutorial first.

## What You'll Learn[¶](#what-youll-learn)

- How the loss decomposes into:
  - **Reconstruction loss** (`recon_loss`)
  - **Mutual information** (`mut_info_loss`)
  - **Total correlation** (`tot_corr_loss`)
  - **Dimension-wise KL divergence** (`dimwise_kl_loss`)
- How annealing can be applied to disentanglement weights (`beta_mi`, `beta_tc`, `beta_dimKL`)
- How to initialize, run and visualize a disentangled VAE

## 1) Loss Decomposition[¶](#1-loss-decomposition)

The `DisentanglixLoss` class computes the following terms for each batch:

1. **Reconstruction Loss** (`recon_loss`)\
   Measures how well the decoded output matches the input.
1. **Mutual Information Loss** (`mut_info_loss`)\
   Encourages each latent dimension to encode information about the inputs.
1. **Total Correlation Loss** (`tot_corr_loss`)\
   Penalizes correlations between latent dimensions to encourage independence.
1. **Dimension-wise KL Loss** (`dimwise_kl_loss`)\
   Regularizes each latent dimension individually against the prior.

The total loss is computed as a weighted sum:

```
total_loss = recon_loss 
             + beta_mi * mut_info_loss 
             + beta_tc * tot_corr_loss 
             + beta_dimKL * dimwise_kl_loss
```

## 2) Annealing[¶](#2-annealing)

Disentanglix supports flexible annealing strategies:

- no-annealing: uses constant weights throughout training
- Custom annealing functions: scales the disentanglement weights according to the current epoch

Annealing is applied independently to each loss term, allowing smooth transitions between reconstruction-focused and disentanglement-focused training.

## Requirements 1: Be in the correct directory (execute below)[¶](#requirements-1-be-in-the-correct-directory-execute-below)

## Requirements 2: Obtain tutorial data or use own data[¶](#requirements-2-obtain-tutorial-data-or-use-own-data)

We use real human lung single-cell RNA-seq data assembled from the [CZ CELLxGENE Census](https://cellxgene.cziscience.com/). It is hosted on Hugging Face Hub ([autoencodix/census-lung](https://huggingface.co/datasets/autoencodix/census-lung)) and is downloaded automatically in the cells below on first run. The full dataset contains ~89,000 cells spanning four lung cell types (malignant cells, pulmonary alveolar type 2 cells, respiratory basal cells, alveolar macrophages), which also correlate closely with the `disease` metadata column (normal / lung adenocarcinoma / cystic fibrosis). We use `cell_type` and `disease` as the two factors to inspect for disentanglement below. To keep this tutorial fast to run, we draw a balanced subsample of 2,000 cells per cell type.

## 3) Initialize and Run Disentanglix[¶](#3-initialize-and-run-disentanglix)

This works like `Varix`, except we don't have one `beta` parameter to weight the distribution loss, we have three `betas` one for each sub loss term which we can set a value for in the config.

In \[3\]:

Copied!

```
import numpy as np
import anndata as ad
import mudata

from autoencodix.configs.disentanglix_config import DisentanglixConfig
from autoencodix.configs.default_config import DataCase, DataConfig, DataInfo
from autoencodix.data.datapackage import DataPackage
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
import autoencodix as acx

sc_path = hf_hub_download(
    repo_id="autoencodix/census-lung", repo_type="dataset", filename="census_lung.h5ad"
)
full_adata = ad.read_h5ad(sc_path)

# Balanced subsample: 2,000 cells per cell type keeps the tutorial fast to run
# while keeping all four (well-separated) cell types equally represented.
N_PER_TYPE = 2000
rng = np.random.RandomState(43)
subsample_idx = []
for _, group in full_adata.obs.groupby("cell_type", observed=True):
    n = min(N_PER_TYPE, len(group))
    subsample_idx.extend(rng.choice(group.index.values, size=n, replace=False))

adata = full_adata[subsample_idx].copy()

sc_data = DataPackage()
sc_data.multi_sc = {"multi_sc": mudata.MuData({"rna": adata})}

my_cfg = DisentanglixConfig(
	data_case=DataCase.MULTI_SINGLE_CELL,
	loss_reduction="sum",
	k_filter=2000,
	latent_dim=2,
	scaling="STANDARD",
	epochs=50,
	learning_rate=0.01,
	batch_size = 128,
	beta_mi = 0.1,
	beta_tc = 0.1,
	beta_dimKL= 0.1,
	use_mss = True,
	drop_p =0.1,
	global_seed=7,
	reproducible=True,
	checkpoint_interval=10,
	n_layers=1,
	annotation_columns=["cell_type", "disease"],
	data_config=DataConfig(
		data_info={"multi_sc": DataInfo(is_single_cell=True, data_type="NUMERIC")},
	),
)

disent = acx.Disentanglix(data=sc_data, config=my_cfg)
```

### Comparing a Second `beta_tc` Setting[¶](#comparing-a-second-beta_tc-setting)

To show what disentanglement regularization actually does, we run the pipeline a second time with `beta_tc` raised from `0.1` to `100` (`beta_dimKL` is lowered from `0.1` to `0.01` to compensate, keeping the total loss balanced). `beta_tc` weights the total-correlation term, which directly penalizes correlation between latent dimensions. A higher value therefore results in stronger disentanglement.

In \[8\]:

Copied!

```
my_cfg2 = DisentanglixConfig(
	data_case=DataCase.MULTI_SINGLE_CELL,
	loss_reduction="sum",
	k_filter=2000,
	latent_dim=2,
	scaling="STANDARD",
	epochs=50,
	learning_rate=0.01,
	batch_size = 128,
	beta_mi = 0.1,
	beta_tc = 100,
	beta_dimKL= 0.01,
	use_mss = True,
	drop_p =0.1,
	global_seed=7,
	reproducible=True,
	checkpoint_interval=10,
	n_layers=1,
	annotation_columns=["cell_type", "disease"],
	data_config=DataConfig(
		data_info={"multi_sc": DataInfo(is_single_cell=True, data_type="NUMERIC")},
	),
)

disent2 = acx.Disentanglix(data=sc_data, config=my_cfg2)
```

```
print("Model files:", model_files)

disent_loaded = acx.Disentanglix.load(outpath)
```

#### Generate New Data[¶](#generate-new-data)

For a variational autoencoder, the generate or sample_latent_space step draws new latent vectors from the model’s learned latent distribution.

**Latent Sampling:** The model first aggregates the posterior over all encoded latent vectors in the chosen split and epoch by computing the mean (global_mu) and log-variance (global_logvar). It then samples new latent points from a diagonal Gaussian defined by these aggregate statistics, using the reparameterization trick to inject Gaussian noise.

**Number of Samples (n_samples):** Users can specify how many latent points to generate. The method expands the aggregated mean and log-variance to match the requested number of samples before sampling.

**Custom Latent Prior:** Optionally, a custom latent_prior can be provided (a tensor or NumPy array with shape (n_samples, latent_dim)), which will be used directly instead of the aggregated posterior. This is basically the `decode` step.

In \[15\]:

Copied!

```
reconstructions_generated = disent_loaded.generate(n_samples=5)
print(reconstructions_generated.shape)
```

reconstructions_generated = disent_loaded.generate(n_samples=5) print(reconstructions_generated.shape)

```
Reproducibility settings for device auto are not implemented or necessary i.e. for cpu.
torch.Size([5, 2000])
```

> **Note:** This environment variable is required for fully deterministic CuBLAS ops on CUDA >= 10.2 when `reproducible=True` is set below. Without it, PyTorch raises a `RuntimeError` instead of training deterministically. It must be set before `torch` is imported. See the [README FAQ](https://jan-forest.github.io/autoencodix_package/tutorials/README.md#reproducibility-and-cublas_workspace_config) for details.


# How To Use Imagix[¶](#how-to-use-imagix)

Imagix is our implementation of a variational autoencoder for image data.\
This tutorial follows the structure of [`Getting Started - Vanillix`](https://jan-forest.github.io/autoencodix_package/tutorials/PipelineTutorials/Imagix/Vanillix.ipynb), but is much less extensive because our pipeline works similarly across different architectures. Here we focus only on Imagix specifics.

**AUTOENCODIX** supports far more functionality than shown here, so we’ll also point to advanced tutorials where relevant.

**IMPORTANT**

> This tutorial only shows the specifics of the Imagix pipeline. If you're unfamiliar with general concepts,\
> we recommend following the [`Getting Started - Vanillix`](https://jan-forest.github.io/autoencodix_package/tutorials/PipelineTutorials/Imagix/Vanillix.ipynb) Tutorial first.

## What You'll Learn[¶](#what-youll-learn)

You’ll learn how to:

1. **Initialize** the pipeline and run it.
1. Understand the Imagix specific **pipeline steps**.
1. Access the Imagix specific **results** (mus, sigma, kl/mmd losses).
1. **Visualize** outputs effectively.
1. Apply **custom parameters**. or Architecture
1. **Save, load, and reuse** a trained pipeline.

**Setting the Correct Path**

In \[2\]:

## 1) Initialize the Imagix Pipeline[¶](#1-initialize-the-imagix-pipeline)

`Imagix` is a standard VAE implementation for image data. We don't allow different data modalities for `Imagix`.\
To run the pipeline we need to prepare two things:

1. A directory with image files. We allow the following extensions: `".jpg", ".jpeg", ".png", ".tif", ".tiff"` (NOT case sensitive).
1. An annotation file with metadata, where we map `sample_ids` to image paths. For this, we need to provide the name of the column where the image path information is stored. This is done via the `img_paths_col` config parameter.

### ❗❗Requirements ❗❗[¶](#requirements)

The data for this tutorial is hosted on Hugging Face Hub ([autoencodix/mnist](https://huggingface.co/datasets/autoencodix/mnist)) and is downloaded (and extracted) automatically in the cell below on first run.

#### 1.1 The Dataset[¶](#11-the-dataset)

Here we use a balanced subsample of the classic MNIST handwritten digits dataset: 2000 images, 200 per digit (0-9), 28x28 grayscale. The annotation column `label` gives the digit class for each image.

**A Look Inside the Annotation File**:

In \[3\]:

Copied!

```
import os
import zipfile
import pandas as pd
import autoencodix as acx
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from autoencodix.configs.default_config import (
    DefaultConfig,
    DataConfig,
    DataCase,
    DataInfo,
)

IMGMAPPING = hf_hub_download(repo_id="autoencodix/mnist", repo_type="dataset", filename="mnist_mappings.txt")
images_zip = hf_hub_download(repo_id="autoencodix/mnist", repo_type="dataset", filename="mnist_images.zip")

IMGROOT = os.path.join("data/images/mnist_images/")
if not os.path.isdir(IMGROOT):
    with zipfile.ZipFile(images_zip) as zf:
        zf.extractall("data/images/")

anno_df = pd.read_csv(IMGMAPPING, sep="\t", index_col=0)
anno_df.head()
```

import os import zipfile import pandas as pd import autoencodix as acx from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download from autoencodix.configs.default_config import ( DefaultConfig, DataConfig, DataCase, DataInfo, ) IMGMAPPING = hf_hub_download(repo_id="autoencodix/mnist", repo_type="dataset", filename="mnist_mappings.txt") images_zip = hf_hub_download(repo_id="autoencodix/mnist", repo_type="dataset", filename="mnist_images.zip") IMGROOT = os.path.join("data/images/mnist_images/") if not os.path.isdir(IMGROOT): with zipfile.ZipFile(images_zip) as zf: zf.extractall("data/images/") anno_df = pd.read_csv(IMGMAPPING, sep="\\t", index_col=0) anno_df.head()

```
imgconfig = DefaultConfig(
    data_case=DataCase.IMG_TO_IMG,
    checkpoint_interval=25,
    epochs=250,
    reconstruction_loss="bce",
    beta=0.005,
    scaling="MINMAX",
    anneal_function="logistic-late",
    data_config=DataConfig(
        data_info={
            "IMG": DataInfo(
                file_path=IMGROOT,
                scaling="MINMAX",
                data_type="IMG",
            ),
            "ANNO": DataInfo(
                file_path=IMGMAPPING,
                data_type="ANNOTATION",
            ),
        },
    ),
)

imagix = acx.Imagix(config=imgconfig)
result = imagix.run()
backup_datset = result.datasets
```

## 4) Visualize Imagix Results[¶](#4-visualize-imagix-results)

Since the results of `Imagix` are visually interpretable, we add an additional visualization:\
We show a grid of original images and reconstructed images with label information. See the code below for how to obtain this visualization.

Copied!


**Standard Visualizations**\
We also offer the standard visualizations as for all other pipelines. You can pass one or more column names from the annotation data. These columns will be used to color the visualizations accordingly. In this example, we use the `label` parameter.

## 5) Customize Imagix[¶](#5-customize-imagix)

Via the `Config` object we can apply customize the pipeline by chaning the `loss function` or the number of `epoch` or preprocessing. To get an full overview of the adjustable parameters, please refere to [2].\
In Addition, there is a way to use another architecture for the image autoencoder. We currently offer two architectures:`ImageVAEArchitecture` and `ImageVAEFastArchitecture`. The fast architecture does not has BatchNorm and inplace activation functions, which can speed up the training process. The `ImageVAEArchitecture` is the default architecture and based on [Yang & Uhler](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.03515).

We can simply pass the architecture as type to the `model_type` parameter of the `Imagix` pipeline.

[2] [Tutorials/DeepDives/ConfigTutorial.ipynb](https://jan-forest.github.io/autoencodix_package/tutorials/PipelineTutorials/DeepDives/ConfigTutorial.ipynb).

In \[8\]:

Copied!

```
from autoencodix.modeling._imgfast_architecture import ImageVAEFastArchitecture
from autoencodix.modeling._imagevae_architecture import ImageVAEArchitecture


imgconfig = DefaultConfig(
    data_case=DataCase.IMG_TO_IMG,
    checkpoint_interval=25,
    epochs=250,
    reconstruction_loss="bce",
    beta=0.005,
    scaling="MINMAX",
    anneal_function="logistic-late",
    data_config=DataConfig(
        data_info={
            "IMG": DataInfo(
                file_path=IMGROOT,
                scaling="MINMAX",
                data_type="IMG",
            ),
            "ANNO": DataInfo(
                file_path=IMGMAPPING,
                data_type="ANNOTATION",
            ),
        },
    ),
)

imagix = acx.Imagix(config=imgconfig, model_type=ImageVAEFastArchitecture)
result = imagix.run()
backup_datset = result.datasets
```

## 6) Load Save and Reuse Imagix[¶](#6-load-save-and-reuse-imagix)

There are not `Imagix` specific steps here. See the `Getting Started - Vanillix` for details. Below is a basic save/load usecase.

In \[9\]:

Copied!

```
import os
import glob

outpath = os.path.join("tutorial_res", "imagix.pkl")

imagix.save(file_path=outpath)

folder = os.path.dirname(outpath)
pkl_files = glob.glob(os.path.join(folder, "*imagix.pkl"))
model_files = glob.glob(os.path.join(folder, "*imagix.pth"))

print("PKL files:", pkl_files)
print("Model files:", model_files)

# the load functionality automatically will build the pipeline object out of the three saved files
imagix_loaded = acx.Imagix.load(outpath)
```

import os import glob outpath = os.path.join("tutorial_res", "imagix.pkl") imagix.save(file_path=outpath) folder = os.path.dirname(outpath) pkl_files = glob.glob(os.path.join(folder, "\*imagix.pkl")) model_files = glob.glob(os.path.join(folder, "\*imagix.pth")) print("PKL files:", pkl_files) print("Model files:", model_files)

# the load functionality automatically will build the pipeline object out of the three saved files

imagix_loaded = acx.Imagix.load(outpath)

# How To Use Imagix3D[¶](#how-to-use-imagix3d)

Imagix3D is an implementation of a variational autoencoder for 3D image data (volumes).\
This tutorial follows the structure of [`Getting Started - Vanillix`](https://jan-forest.github.io/autoencodix_package/tutorials/PipelineTutorials/Imagix3D/Vanillix.ipynb), and repeats many of the parts therein which cover the general functionaliy of the **AUTOENCODIX** framework. The aim is to provide a tutorial for Imagix3D that simultaneously functions as

- a general demonstration of basic **AUTOENCODIX** functionalities
- a specific tutorial about the 3D image pipeline workflow
- an end-to-end test for Imagix3D that covers all its functionalities

**NOTE:** This tutorial is very similar to the one for [`Getting Started - Imagix`](https://jan-forest.github.io/autoencodix_package/tutorials/PipelineTutorials/Imagix3D/Imagix.ipynb). So if you already did the `Imagix` tutorial, this one should be easy to follow.

## What You'll Learn[¶](#what-youll-learn)

You’ll learn how to:

1. **Initialize** the pipeline and run it.
1. Understand the Imagix specific **pipeline steps**.
1. Access the Imagix specific **results** (mus, sigma, kl/mmd losses).
1. **Visualize** outputs effectively.
1. Apply **custom parameters**. or Architecture
1. **Save, load, and reuse** a trained pipeline.

**Setting the Correct Path**

In \[2\]:

Copied!

```
import os

p = os.getcwd()
d = "autoencodix_package"
if d not in p:
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"'{d}' not found in path: {p}")
os.chdir(os.sep.join(p.split(os.sep)[: p.split(os.sep).index(d) + 1]))
print(f"Changed to: {os.getcwd()}")
```

## 1) Initialize the Imagix3D Pipeline[¶](#1-initialize-the-imagix3d-pipeline)

`Imagix3D` is a VAE implementation for 3D image data. Other data modalities are not allowed for `Imagix3D` (including 2D image data).\
This tutorial will be restricted to 3D human medical imaging data. However, the pipeline also works for other 3D data, provided that they come in a data type which is allwed (see down below). To run the pipeline we need to prepare two things:

1. A directory with image files. The following extensions are allowed: `".nii", ".nii.gz"` (for the time being - this might change in the future).
1. An annotation file with metadata, where we map `sample_ids` to image paths. For this, we need to provide the name of the column where the image path information is stored. This is done via the `img_path_col` config parameter.
1. A configuration object

### ❗❗Requirements ❗❗[¶](#requirements)

The data for this tutorial is hosted on Hugging Face Hub ([autoencodix/mnist](https://huggingface.co/datasets/autoencodix/mnist)) and is downloaded (and extracted) automatically in the cell below on first run.

#### 1.1 📊 The Dataset[¶](#11-the-dataset)

Here we use a subsample of the OrganMNIST3D dataset, which is part of MedMNIST collection (see <https://medmnist.com/>). The original OrganMNIST3D is comprised of abdominal computed tomography (CT) scans and includes the organ types: femure-right/left, bladder, liver, spleen, kidney-right/left, lung-right/left, pancreas and heart. The subsample used here only contains the organs femur-right and bladder, and was drawn across train, validation and test splits.

**data:** 345 images, where 174 are bladder and 171 are femure-right organs, 64x64x64 grayscale. The annotation column `group` gives the organ category for each image.

**NOTE:** Since the data were drawn across pre-defined splits and this pipeline does not use custom-splits, the train\_, valid\_ and test\_ prefixes do not indicate in which split they will be assigned to in the Imagix3D pipeline. They were merely drawn across splits to have enough data of a dataset with a binary category of organ labels that are very distinct.

**A Look Inside the Annotation File**:

In \[3\]:

Copied!

```
import os
import zipfile
import pandas as pd
import autoencodix as acx
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from autoencodix.configs.imagix3d_config import Imagix3DConfig
from autoencodix.configs.default_config import (
    DataConfig,
    DataCase,
    DataInfo
)


IMGMAPPING = hf_hub_download(
    repo_id="autoencodix/OrganMNIST3D-subsample",
    repo_type="dataset",
    filename="organmnist3d_mappings.csv",
)

zip_path = hf_hub_download(
    repo_id="autoencodix/OrganMNIST3D-subsample",
    repo_type="dataset",
    filename="organmnist3d_images.zip",
)

VOLIMAGES = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(zip_path), "images")

os.makedirs(VOLIMAGES, exist_ok=True)

with zipfile.ZipFile(zip_path) as zf:
    zf.extractall(VOLIMAGES)

anno_df = pd.read_csv(IMGMAPPING, sep=",", index_col=0)
anno_df.head()
```

import os import zipfile import pandas as pd import autoencodix as acx from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download from autoencodix.configs.imagix3d_config import Imagix3DConfig from autoencodix.configs.default_config import ( DataConfig, DataCase, DataInfo ) IMGMAPPING = hf_hub_download( repo_id="autoencodix/OrganMNIST3D-subsample", repo_type="dataset", filename="organmnist3d_mappings.csv", ) zip_path = hf_hub_download( repo_id="autoencodix/OrganMNIST3D-subsample", repo_type="dataset", filename="organmnist3d_images.zip", ) VOLIMAGES = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(zip_path), "images") os.makedirs(VOLIMAGES, exist_ok=True) with zipfile.ZipFile(zip_path) as zf: zf.extractall(VOLIMAGES) anno_df = pd.read_csv(IMGMAPPING, sep=",", index_col=0) anno_df.head()

#### 1.2 ⚙️ Configuration Object[¶](#12-configuration-object)

We use the default parameters in `Imagix3DConfig`.\
Additionally, we define a `DataCase`, which tells the pipeline what kind of data to expect.\
In this case: `IMG`.

**Define Config**

In \[4\]:

Copied!

```
volconfig = Imagix3DConfig(
    data_case=DataCase.IMG_TO_IMG,
    img_path_col="filepath",
    spatial_shape_policy="crop_or_pad_to_shape",
    target_shape_3d=(64,64,64),
    checkpoint_interval=10,
    epochs=100,
    learning_rate=0.0005,
    reconstruction_loss="mse",
    beta=0.001,
    scaling="MINMAX",
    anneal_function="logistic-late",
    data_config=DataConfig(
        data_info={
            "IMG": DataInfo(
                file_path=os.path.join(VOLIMAGES, "organmnist3d_subsample"),
                scaling="MINMAX",
                data_type="IMG",
            ),
            "ANNO": DataInfo(
                file_path=IMGMAPPING,
                data_type="ANNOTATION",
            ),
        },
    ),
)

imagix3d = acx.Imagix3D(config=volconfig)
result = imagix3d.run()
backup_dataset = result.datasets
```

## 2) Understand Imagix3D Specific Steps[¶](#2-understand-imagix3d-specific-steps)

Since `Imagix3D` is just a `Imagix` for volumes, which in turn is just a `Varix` for images, there are no extra steps for this pipeline.

## 3) Visualize Imagix3D Results[¶](#3-visualize-imagix3d-results)

Since the results of `Imagix3D` are visually interpretable, we add an additional visualization:\
We show a grid of

- original images
- reconstructed images
- and error images (subtraction between the two) with label information on top.

Because these are 3D images, the 2D depictions only show slices from a certain orientation. Therefore the 3D images are shown from the

- axial ('top to bottom'),
- coronal ('front to back'), and
- sagittal ('right to left') orientation.

See the code below for how to obtain this visualization.

In \[5\]:

Copied!

```
imagix3d.visualizer.show_image_recon_grid(
    result=imagix3d.result, 
    n_samples=5)
```

imagix3d.visualizer.show_image_recon_grid( result=imagix3d.result, n_samples=5)

By passing the keyword argument `params` and providing a list of columns from the annotation data, you get visualizations based on these columns. In this example, we use the `group` parameter.\
Refer to [5] for more details on how to work with plots.

## 3) Access Imagix Specific Results[¶](#3-access-imagix-specific-results)

In contrast to `Imagix`, `Imagix3D` does provide pipeline specific results for volumes.

#### Comparing reconstructions to originals, wrt the best, median and worst examples[¶](#comparing-reconstructions-to-originals-wrt-the-best-median-and-worst-examples)

Instead of looking at reconstrunction success from randomly drawn samples, we can here check for the best, median and worst reconstruction cases from our pipeline

```
    result=imagix3d.result,
    selection="bmw",
    metric="mse")
```

#### Correlations between latent dimensions[¶](#correlations-between-latent-dimensions)

This visualization shows pairwise `correlations between latent dimensions` to assess how strongly they encode overlapping information.

The optional table and correlation matrix provide a numerical and visual overview of these relationships, where high absolute correlations indicate less independent latent dimensions.

In \[8\]:

Copied!

```
imagix3d.visualizer.show_latent_corr(
    result=imagix3d.result,
    show_table=False,
    show_corrmat=True)
```

imagix3d.visualizer.show_latent_corr( result=imagix3d.result, show_table=False, show_corrmat=True)

#### Inspect latent dimension "activity"[¶](#inspect-latent-dimension-activity)

First defined by Burda et al. (2015)[1](#fn1) and later taken up by Sinha & Dieng (2021)[2](#fn2) the **activity** of the dimension of the latent variables **z** is (Var(x) > \\delta) , where (\\delta) is a user-defined threshold set to 0.01 in the papers. An active dimension is termed an *active unit* in Sinha & Dieng. If the variance of a given dimension is very low it indicates that this very dimension is not used / inactive. The higher the number of latent active units, the better the learned representations.

**compute latent activity...**

In \[9\]:

Copied!

```
imagix3d.results = imagix3d.evaluator.compute_latent_activity(
    result=imagix3d.result,
    threshold=0.01,
    splits=("train", "valid"),
    include_test=True)
```

imagix3d.results = imagix3d.evaluator.compute_latent_activity( result=imagix3d.result, threshold=0.01, splits=("train", "valid"), include_test=True)

**...and show the results**

In \[10\]:

Copied!

```
imagix3d.visualizer.show_latent_activity(
    result=imagix3d.result,
    show_table=False,
    show_dim_table=False)
```

imagix3d.visualizer.show_latent_activity( result=imagix3d.result, show_table=False, show_dim_table=False)

#### Latent Traversal[¶](#latent-traversal)

We can use latent traversal as a qualitative visualization technique to inspect what individual latent dimensions have learned to represent. Starting from a fixed latent vector, one latent dimension is varied while all other dimensions are held constant, and the decoder generates the corresponding output images. If changing a specific latent dimension produces changes in the reconstructed volume, this suggests that the dimension captures a meaningful factor of variation in the data.

**Compute latent traversal...**

In \[11\]:

Copied!

```
imagix3d.result =imagix3d.evaluator.compute_latent_traversal(
    result=imagix3d.result,
    latent_dims="top_kl",
    n_latent_dims=8,
    value_mode="percentile",
    n_values=5)
```

imagix3d.result =imagix3d.evaluator.compute_latent_traversal( result=imagix3d.result, latent_dims="top_kl", n_latent_dims=8, value_mode="percentile", n_values=5)

**...and show the results**

In \[12\]:

## 5) Customize Imagix3D[¶](#5-customize-imagix3d)

To customize the behavior of our pipeline, you adjust the configuration.\
There are two ways to work with the config:

1. Create a customized instance of the config class.
1. Provide a `yaml` file and use the config class to read it.

We will focus on option 1 and show a few examples. Via the `Config` object we can apply customize the pipeline by chaning the `loss function` or the number of `epoch` or preprocessing. To get an full overview of the adjustable parameters, please refere to [2].

In Addition, there is a way to use another architecture for the image autoencoder. We currently offer two architectures:`VolumeVAEArchitecture` and `VolumeVAEFastArchitecture`. The fast architecture does not has BatchNorm and inplace activation functions, which can speed up the training process. The `VolumeVAEArchitecture` is the default architecture.

We can simply pass the architecture as type to the `model_type` parameter of the `Imagix3D` pipeline.

[2] Tutorials/DeepDives/ConfigTutorial.ipynb.

In \[14\]:

Copied!

```
from autoencodix.modeling._volfast_architecture import VolumeVAEFastArchitecture
from autoencodix.modeling._volumevae_architecture import VolumeVAEArchitecture

custom_volconfig = Imagix3DConfig(
    data_case=DataCase.IMG_TO_IMG,
    img_path_col="filepath",
    spatial_shape_policy="crop_or_pad_to_shape",
    target_shape_3d=(64,64,64),
    checkpoint_interval=10,
    epochs=100,
    learning_rate=0.001,
    reconstruction_loss="mse",
    beta=0.005,
    scaling="MINMAX",
    anneal_function="logistic-late",
    data_config=DataConfig(
        data_info={
            "IMG": DataInfo(
                file_path=os.path.join(VOLIMAGES, "organmnist3d_subsample"),
                scaling="MINMAX",
                data_type="IMG",
            ),
            "ANNO": DataInfo(
                file_path=IMGMAPPING,
                data_type="ANNOTATION",
            ),
        },
    ),
)

imagix3d = acx.Imagix3D(
    config=custom_volconfig, 
    model_type=VolumeVAEFastArchitecture
)
result = imagix3d.run()
backup_dataset = result.datasets
```

## 6) Load Save and Reuse Imagix3D[¶](#6-load-save-and-reuse-imagix3d)

Lastly, we show how to re-use a trained pipeline, as well as how to save and load it.\
You can do the following:

- Use the trained pipeline to run the `predict` step with new data.
- Obtain the latent space, apply transformations, and run the `decode` step of the trained pipeline.
- Generate new data by computing the mean and standard deviation of all encoded latent vectors in the chosen split and epoch, fitting a diagonal Gaussian to those statistics, and sampling new latent points by adding scaled Gaussian noise to that mean.
- Access the underlying PyTorch model and re-use it in any way you like.
- Store the pipeline on disk or in the cloud, then reload it and continue using it

#### Save and Load[¶](#save-and-load)

Best practice is to provide a file path without extension, we set the extensions internally and handle all saving and loading.

In \[15\]:

Copied!

```
import os
import glob

outpath = os.path.join("tutorial_res", "imagix3d.pkl")

imagix3d.save(file_path=outpath,
             save_all=True)

folder = os.path.dirname(outpath)
pkl_files = glob.glob(os.path.join(folder, "*imagix3d.pkl"))
model_files = glob.glob(os.path.join(folder, "*imagix3d.pth"))

print("PKL files:", pkl_files)
print("Model files:", model_files)

# the load functionality automatically will build the pipeline object out of the three saved files
imagix3d_loaded = acx.Imagix3D.load(outpath)
```

import os import glob outpath = os.path.join("tutorial_res", "imagix3d.pkl") imagix3d.save(file_path=outpath, save_all=True) folder = os.path.dirname(outpath) pkl_files = glob.glob(os.path.join(folder, "\*imagix3d.pkl")) model_files = glob.glob(os.path.join(folder, "\*imagix3d.pth")) print("PKL files:", pkl_files) print("Model files:", model_files)

# How To Use Maskix[¶](#how-to-use-maskix)

Maskix is our implementation of a variational autoencoder.\
This tutorial follows the structure of our `Getting Started - Vanillix`, but is much less extensive, because\
our pipeline works similarly for different architectures, so here we focus only on Maskix specifics.

**AUTOENCODIX** supports far more functionality than shown here, so we’ll also point to advanced tutorials where relevant.

**IMPORTANT**

> This tutorial only shows the specifics of the Maskix pipeline. If you're unfamiliar with general concepts,\
> we recommend following the [`Getting Started - Vanillix`](https://jan-forest.github.io/autoencodix_package/tutorials/PipelineTutorials/Maskix/Vanillix.ipynb) tutorial first.

## What You'll Learn[¶](#what-youll-learn)

You’ll learn how to:

1. **Theory primer** of the Maskix architecture.
1. **Initialize** the pipeline and run the pipeline.
1. Understand Maskix-specific \**config parameters*.
1. **Access & Visualize** the results effectively.
1. Pass **custom masking fucntions**.
1. How to use Maskix for **data imputation**
1. **Save, load, and reuse** a trained pipeline.

## 1) Theory Primer[¶](#1-theory-primer)

Maskix adapts the scMAE (single-cell Masked Autoencoder) framework from Fang et al. (2024) for single-cell RNA-seq analysis. The model learns useful representations by corrupting the input expression matrix and training the network both to reconstruct the original data and to identify which entries were perturbed. This encourages the model to capture gene–gene (or feature–feature) relationships in high-dimensional, noisy datasets. Although originally designed for single-cell data, the same approach applies to other domains.

Each training iteration follows this corruption process:

1. Sample a Bernoulli distribution to determine which entries should be perturbed, producing a binary mask with the same shape as the input.
1. For each gene (or feature), generate a random permutation of sample indices.
1. For all positions marked as masked, replace the original value with the value from the permuted index for that feature.

The corrupted input is encoded into a low-dimensional latent representation. In parallel, a mask predictor takes the latent space as input and estimates which positions were masked. The predicted mask is then concatenated with the latent representation and passed into a decoder that attempts to reconstruct the original values.

Training uses two loss components. The mask predictor is optimized with binary cross-entropy against the true mask. Reconstruction uses a weighted mean-squared error where masked entries receive higher weight, controlled by the hyperparameter `delta_mask_corrupted`. The total loss is the weighted sum of these components, balanced by the hyperparameter `delta_mask_predictor`.

## Requirements 1: Be in the correct directory (execute below)[¶](#requirements-1-be-in-the-correct-directory-execute-below)

## Requirements 2: Obtain tutorial data or use own data[¶](#requirements-2-obtain-tutorial-data-or-use-own-data)

We use a dataset from [Fang et al. (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btae020), originally the human pancreas scRNA-seq data from Baron et al. (2016), GEO accession GSE84133. It is hosted on Hugging Face Hub ([autoencodix/pancreas-fang](https://huggingface.co/datasets/autoencodix/pancreas-fang)) and is downloaded automatically in the cells below on first run — no manual download or placement into `data/raw` needed. Alternatively you can use your own single-cell dataset (Maskix works with other datatypes, but in this example we expect single cell data: `h5ad`) file and replace the variable `sc_path`.

## 2) Initialize and Run Maskix[¶](#2-initialize-and-run-maskix)

As for every other pipline, we need to perform the following steps:

- import relevant classes
- define a config
- init the pipeline
- call the run step

In \[3\]:

Copied!

```
import autoencodix as acx
from autoencodix.configs import MaskixConfig
from autoencodix.configs.default_config import DataInfo, DataConfig, DataCase

from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download

sc_path = hf_hub_download(
    repo_id="autoencodix/pancreas-fang", repo_type="dataset", filename="pancreas.h5ad"
)
config = MaskixConfig(
    epochs=30,
    checkpoint_interval=10,
    k_filter=1000,
    batch_size=128,
    annotation_columns=["assigned_cluster"],
    data_config=DataConfig(        
        data_info={
            "multi_sc": DataInfo(
                file_path=sc_path, is_single_cell=True, data_type="NUMERIC"
            )
        },
    ),
    data_case=DataCase.MULTI_SINGLE_CELL,
)
maskix= acx.Maskix(config=config)
```

## 3) Understanding Maskix-specific Config Parameters[¶](#3-understanding-maskix-specific-config-parameters)

As described in the [theory section](#1-theory-primer), we implemented the architecture from [Fang et al. (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btae020), with weighted loss terms and a specific encoder–decoder design. To make this adaptable within our framework, we expose the following configuration parameters:

- **maskix_hidden_dim**: Hidden dimension used in the Maskix encoder and decoder, matching the scMAE reference architecture by default.
- **maskix_swap_prob**: Bernoulli probability controlling how often feature values are swapped during input corruption.
- **delta_mask_predictor**: Weighting factor for the mask prediction loss in the total training objective.
- **delta_mask_corrupted**: Weighting factor that increases the reconstruction penalty on corrupted entries.
- **maskix_architecture**: Selects between the default scMAE architecture or a custom architecture configured through `n_layers` and `enc_factor`.

You can find the default values by running the following:

In \[5\]:

Copied!

```
MaskixConfig.print_schema(
    filter_params=[
        "maskix_hidden_dim",
        "maskix_swap_prob",
        "delta_mask_predictor",
        "delta_mask_corrupted",
        "maskix_architecture",
    ]
)
```

MaskixConfig.print_schema( filter_params=[ "maskix_hidden_dim", "maskix_swap_prob", "delta_mask_predictor", "delta_mask_corrupted", "maskix_architecture", ] )

```
Valid Keyword Arguments:
--------------------------------------------------

maskix_hidden_dim:
  Type: <class 'int'>
  Default: 128
  Description: The Maskix implementation follows https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btae020. The authors use a hidden dimension 0f 256 for their neural network, so we set this as default

maskix_swap_prob:
  Type: <class 'float'>
  Default: 0.2
  Description: For the Maskix input_data masinkg, we sample a probablity if samples within one gene should be swapt. This is done with a Bernoulli distribution, maskix_swap_prob is the probablity passed to the bernoulli distribution 

delta_mask_predictor:
  Type: <class 'float'>
  Default: 0.7
  Description: Delta weighting factor of the mask prediction loss term for the Maskix

delta_mask_corrupted:
  Type: <cla
... [output truncated]
```

## 4) Access & Visualize Results Effectively[¶](#4-access-visualize-results-effectively)

In addition to the results that the Vanillix pipeline provided, we can access:

- `total`, `reconstruction`, and `masked` losses

A note on the different loss types:\
For our maksed autoencoder, the total loss consists of a reconstruction loss and a mask predictor los To investigate these losses, the `result` object has the attribute `sub_losses`.\
This is a `LossRegistry` with the name of the loss as the key, and the value is a `TrainingDynamics` object, which can be accessed in the same way as for the Vanillix results.

For more details, check [`Tutorials/DeepDives/PipelineOutputTutorial.ipynb`](https://jan-forest.github.io/autoencodix_package/tutorials/PipelineTutorials/DeepDives/PipelineOutputTutorial.ipynb).

In \[6\]:

Copied!

```
sub_losses = maskix_result.sub_losses
print("Sub Losses:")
print(f"keys: {sub_losses.keys()}")
print("\n")
recon_dyn = sub_losses.get(key="recon_loss")
print("Value of reconstruction loss in epoch 4 for train split")
print(recon_dyn.get(split="train", epoch=4))
```

## 5) Adding a Custom Masking Function to `MaskixTrainer`[¶](#5-adding-a-custom-masking-function-to-maskixtrainer)

`MaskixTrainer` supports replacing its default corruption mechanism with a user-defined masking function. This enables experimentation with alternative masking strategies while ensuring compatibility with the trainer’s data flow.

#### How to Add a Custom Masking Function[¶](#how-to-add-a-custom-masking-function)

Provide your masking function at initialization:

```
# We assume that config is defined and other imports are done (see above)

def my_masking_fn(x: torch.Tensor, strength: float = 0.2):
    noise = torch.randn_like(x) * strength
    return x + noise  # must return ONLY a single tensor in shape of input tensor

masking_fn_kwargs = {"strength": 0.1}
maskix = acx.Maskix(config=config, masking_fn, masking_fn_kwargs
)
```

#### Requirements for a Custom Masking Function[¶](#requirements-for-a-custom-masking-function)

A custom masking function must satisfy the following constraints:

1. **It must accept a `torch.Tensor` as the first positional argument.**\
   The trainer passes the input mini-batch `X` directly into the function.
1. **It must return exactly one value: a `torch.Tensor`.**\
   The trainer does not consume or propagate additional outputs.\
   Returning tuples or multiple values is not allowed.
1. **The returned tensor must have the same shape as the input tensor.**\
   Any shape mismatch will raise a validation error.
1. **The function must operate on the device of the input tensor.**\
   The function must not assume the tensor resides on the CPU; it must operate on the device of `x`.
1. **Any additional parameters must be passed via `masking_fn_kwargs`.**\
   These keyword arguments provide a clean separation between trainer configuration and masking logic.

##### Example[¶](#example)

This is our default masking method:

```
    def _maskix_hook(
        self, X: torch.Tensor
    ) -> torch.Tensor
        # expand probablities for bernoulli sampling to match input shape
        probs = self._mask_probas.expand(X.shape)

        # Create the Boolean Mask (1 = Swap, 0 = Keep)
        should_swap = torch.bernoulli(probs).bool()

        # COLUMN-WISE SHUFFLING
        # We generate a random float matrix and argsort it along dim=0.
        # This gives us independent random indices for every column.
        rand_indices = torch.rand(X.shape, device=X.device).argsort(dim=0)

        # Use gather to reorder X based on these random indices
        shuffled_X = torch.gather(X, 0, rand_indices)
        corrupted_X = torch.where(should_swap, shuffled_X, X)

        return corrupted_X
```

##### Code Example[¶](#code-example)

In \[8\]:

Copied!

```
import torch
import autoencodix as acx
from autoencodix.configs import MaskixConfig
from autoencodix.configs.default_config import DataInfo, DataConfig, DataCase


def my_masking_fn(x: torch.Tensor, strength: float = 0.2):
    # Noise is created with the same shape, dtype, and device as `x`
    # Because of randn_lie, if you use other function, take care of 
    # device and dtype casting.
    noise = torch.randn_like(x) * strength
    return x + noise


kwargs = {"strength": 0.5}


from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download

sc_path = hf_hub_download(
    repo_id="autoencodix/pancreas-fang", repo_type="dataset", filename="pancreas.h5ad"
)
config = MaskixConfig(
    epochs=30,
    checkpoint_interval=10,
    k_filter=1000,
    batch_size=128,
    data_config=DataConfig(
        annotation_columns=["assigned_cluster"],
        data_info={
            "multi_sc": DataInfo(
                file_path=sc_path, is_single_cell=True, data_type="NUMERIC"
            )
        },
    ),
    data_case=DataCase.MULTI_SINGLE_CELL,
)
```

## 6) Use Maskix to Impute Data[¶](#6-use-maskix-to-impute-data)

You can also input corrupted/missing data and use `Maskix` to impute the data. Here we recommend using a custom masking function. For example, if you want to impute missing values, an imputer could randomly replace values with zeros.

Then you could use `Maskix` to clean your data and use the cleaned data to run your analysis, for example another autoencodix pipeline or anything else. In our mock example we will do the following:

- Create corrupted data with missing values
- Remove the "missing" data
- Train Maskix with clean data, but with a custom imputer that mimics missing data
- Feed corrupted data into trained Maskix and obtain imputed data
- Train Varix with:
  - Original data with missing values
  - Imputed data
- Compare results

#### Create Corrupted Data[¶](#create-corrupted-data)

We will use our single-cell example from before and use maskix to preprocess the data, which makes the artificall corruption process more robust, because we make sure to corrupt informative features/samples.

## [¶](#)

```
import torch
import copy
from autoencodix.data._numeric_dataset import NumericDataset
def drop_samples(ds: NumericDataset):
    """Randomly drops samples in .data and according .metadata (pd.DataFrame) and sample_ids"""
    data = ds.data
    n_samples = data.shape[0]
    drop_prob = 0.3
    keep_mask = torch.bernoulli((1 - drop_prob) * torch.ones(n_samples)).bool()
    # replace entries with zero
    imputed_data = data.clone()
    imputed_data[~keep_mask] = 0

    missing_data = data[keep_mask]
    missing_metadata = ds.metadata.iloc[keep_mask.cpu().numpy()].reset_index(drop=True)
    missing_sample_ids = [sid for i, sid in enumerate(ds.sample_ids) if keep_mask[i]]
    ds_with_missing = copy.deepcopy(ds)
    ds_with_missing.data = missing_data
    ds_with_missing.metadata = missing_metadata
    ds_with_missing.sample_ids = missing_sample_ids


    ds_with_zero = copy.deepcopy(ds)
    ds_with_zero.data = imputed_data
    ds_with_zero.metadata = ds.metadata
    ds_with_zero.sample_ids = ds.sample_ids
    return ds_with_missing, ds_with_zero

ds_with_missing = copy.deepcopy(data)
ds_with_zero = copy.deepcopy(data)
missing_train, ds_with_zero_train = drop_samples(ds_with_missing.train)

print(f"Original train data shape: {data.train.data.shape}, shape after corruption: {missing_train.data.shape}")
missing_test, ds_with_zero_test = drop_samples(data.test)
print(f"Original test data shape: {data.test.data.shape}, shape after corruption: {missing_test.data.shape}")
missing_valid, ds_with_zero_valid    = drop_samples(data.valid)
print(f"Original valid data shape: {data.valid.data.shape}, shape after corruption: {missing_valid.data.shape}")
ds_with_missing.train= missing_train
ds_with_missing.test = missing_test
ds_with_missing.valid = missing_valid


ds_with_zero.train= ds_with_zero_train
ds_with_zero.test = ds_with_zero_test
ds_with_zero.valid = ds_with_zero_valid
# clean corruped samples by removing zero values from dataset (drop samples) and also
```

```
import torch
import autoencodix as acx
from autoencodix.configs import MaskixConfig
from autoencodix.configs.default_config import DataInfo, DataConfig, DataCase


def my_imputer(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    "randomly replaces value with zero"
    rand_mask = torch.bernoulli(0.3 * torch.ones(x.shape, device=x.device)).bool()
    rand_mask.to(x.device)
    imputed_x = torch.where(rand_mask, torch.zeros_like(x, device=x.device), x)
    return imputed_x


from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download

sc_path = hf_hub_download(
    repo_id="autoencodix/pancreas-fang", repo_type="dataset", filename="pancreas.h5ad"
)
config = MaskixConfig(
    epochs=30,
    checkpoint_interval=10,
    k_filter=3000,
    skip_preprocessing=True,
    batch_size=64,
    data_config=DataConfig(
        annotation_columns=["assigned_cluster"],
        data_info={
            "multi_sc": DataInfo(
                 is_single_cell=True, data_type="NUMERIC"
            )
        },
    ),
    data_case=DataCase.MULTI_SINGLE_CELL,
)
maskix = acx.Maskix(config=config, masking_fn=my_imputer, data=ds_with_missing)
result = maskix.run()
```

import torch import autoencodix as acx from autoencodix.configs import MaskixConfig from autoencodix.configs.default_config import DataInfo, DataConfig, DataCase def my_imputer(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: "randomly replaces value with zero" rand_mask = torch.bernoulli(0.3 * torch.ones(x.shape, device=x.device)).bool() rand_mask.to(x.device) imputed_x = torch.where(rand_mask, torch.zeros_like(x, device=x.device), x) return imputed_x from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download sc_path = hf_hub_download( repo_id="autoencodix/pancreas-fang", repo_type="dataset", filename="pancreas.h5ad" ) config = MaskixConfig( epochs=30, checkpoint_interval=10, k_filter=3000, skip_preprocessing=True, batch_size=64, data_config=DataConfig( annotation_columns=["assigned_cluster"], data_info={ "multi_sc": DataInfo( is_single_cell=True, data_type="NUMERIC" ) }, ), data_case=DataCase.MULTI_SINGLE_CELL, ) maskix = acx.Maskix(config=config, masking_fn=my_imputer, data=ds_with_missing) result = maskix.run()

## 7) Save, Load and Re-Use Maskix[¶](#7-save-load-and-re-use-maskix)

There are not `Maskix` specific steps here. See the [`Tutorials/PipelineTutorials/Vanillix.ipynb`](https://jan-forest.github.io/autoencodix_package/tutorials/PipelineTutorials/Maskix/Vanillix.ipynb) or [`Tutorials/DeepDives/MemoryEfficientSaving.ipynb`](https://jan-forest.github.io/autoencodix_package/tutorials/PipelineTutorials/DeepDives/MemoryEfficientSaving.ipynb) for details. Below is a basic save/load usecase:

In \[25\]:

Copied!

```
import os
import glob
# use a filename without extension, we handle this internally
outpath = os.path.join("tutorial_res", "maskix")
maskix.save(file_path=outpath, save_all=False)

folder = os.path.dirname(outpath)
pkl_files = glob.glob(os.path.join(folder, "*.pkl"))
model_files = glob.glob(os.path.join(folder, "*.pth"))

print("PKL files:", pkl_files)
print("Model files:", model_files)

# the load functionality automatically will build the pipeline object out of the three saved files
varix_loaded = acx.Maskix.load(outpath)
varix_loaded.predict(data=maskix_result.datasets)
varix_loaded.visualize()
varix_loaded.show_result()
```

import os import glob

# How to train an ontology-based variational autoencoder (Ontix)[¶](#how-to-train-an-ontology-based-variational-autoencoder-ontix)

In normal autoencoders, latent dimensions are not explainable by design. To gain explainability and incorporate biological information, a popular approach is to restrict the decoder of the autoencoder to match feature connectivity, such as an ontology.

**IMPORTANT**

> This tutorial only shows the specifics of the Ontix pipeline. If you're unfamiliar with general concepts,\
> we recommend following the [`Getting Started - Vanillix`](https://jan-forest.github.io/autoencodix_package/tutorials/PipelineTutorials/Ontix/Vanillix.ipynb) Tutorial first.

## What You'll Learn[¶](#what-youll-learn)

In this notebook we will show two types of ontologies and how they can be used to train an explainable variational autoencoder, `Ontix`. The first is based on biological pathways from the Reactome database (left), and the second uses chromosomal location of genes (right) as a showcase.

You’ll learn how to:

1. **Initialize** the pipeline, ontologies, and run Ontix with **chromosomal ontologies**.
1. **Initialize** the pipeline, ontologies, and run Ontix with **Reactome pathways**.
1. **Evaluate** Ontix on downstream tasks.

By working with these examples, we will also cover on the go:

- Understand the Ontix-specific **pipeline steps**.
- Access the Ontix-specific **results** (mu, sigma, KL/MMD losses).
- **Visualize** outputs effectively.
- Apply **custom parameters**.
- **Save, load, and reuse** a trained pipeline.

### ❗❗ Requirements: Getting Tutorial Data ❗❗[¶](#requirements-getting-tutorial-data)

The data for this tutorial is hosted on Hugging Face Hub ([autoencodix/tcga](https://huggingface.co/datasets/autoencodix/tcga)) and is downloaded automatically in the cells below on first run.

### Extra 2: Get correct path[¶](#extra-2-get-correct-path)

We assume you are in the root of the package. The following code ensures that the correct paths are used. [1] [Tutorials/DeepDives/ConfigTutorial.ipynb](https://jan-forest.github.io/autoencodix_package/tutorials/PipelineTutorials/DeepDives/ConfigTutorial.ipynb)
